virals.name: The Iran Watcher
virals.hook:
The U.S. is considering assassinating top Islamic Republic leaders and “hardliners” to speed up an agreement to end the war.

According to NBC News, supporters believe removing those figures could clear obstacles to a deal and demonstrate to surviving leaders that the U.S. can reach them at any time. Trump has reportedly made no decision.

NBC names no targets. Speculation could focus on Mojtaba Khamenei, IRGC commander Ahmad Vahidi and senior armed-forces figure Keyoumars Heydari. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf could also enter that discussion because of his IRGC background and political influence. None has been publicly confirmed as a target under this proposal.

The U.S. and Israel have already demonstrated their ability to penetrate the regime’s leadership security. Months of CIA and Israeli intelligence gathering helped locate Ali Khamenei and other senior figures. Reuters reported that Israeli intelligence detected a gathering of top officials, allowing the strikes to be timed around it. Khamenei and senior military leaders were killed.

But killing the leadership and changing the regime’s decisions are two different outcomes.

The Islamic Republic’s hostility toward the U.S. and Israel is embedded in its governing ideology, the IRGC and the security apparatus. Officials compete over power and tactics while remaining committed to preserving the same revolutionary system.

Across the 12-day and 40-day wars, Israel and the U.S. inflicted extraordinary losses on the Islamic Republic’s leadership. Israel said it killed more than 30 senior security officials during the 12-day war alone.

The subsequent U.S.-Israeli campaign killed Ali Khamenei and another layer of top military and political figures, demonstrating devastating intelligence penetration of the regime’s highest ranks.

Yet the system elevated Mojtaba Khamenei, replaced its commanders and continued fighting. The ability to eliminate its leaders has repeatedly outpaced the ability to change its decisions.

Removing commanders can disrupt operations, weaken coordination and alter internal calculations. It does not automatically change the institutions that select their replacements or the objectives those institutions pursue.

NBC reports that opponents within the administration fear further assassinations could harden surviving officials’ positions, undermine negotiations and increase threats against American officials.

The U.S. may be able to eliminate more leaders. Whether that produces an agreement depends on who succeeds them, who controls the security apparatus and whether those people have an incentive to compromise.

Masoud Pezeshkian, former foreign minister Mohammad Javad Zarif and former president Hassan Rouhani have repeatedly advocated engagement and an agreement with the U.S. One possible calculation is that removing their rivals could give figures like these greater influence, perhaps even a path to leading the Islamic Republic. That remains an interpretation of the proposal, rather than a succession plan reported by NBC.

Their willingness to negotiate matters. It does not fundamentally change their commitment to preserving the Islamic Republic. An agreement could reflect a different calculation about how to protect the same system, while its ideology, security institutions and mechanisms of repression endure.

Calling certain officials “hardliners” leaves the central question unanswered. What evidence shows that their replacements would make a different choice, and how much would that choice actually change the regime?

virals.hook:
Iranian truck drivers entered a fifth day of strikes on Thursday, with their union saying drivers in 18 cities were refusing to haul freight at rates that have stayed flat as the cost of keeping a truck on the road has climbed.

The strike, which began on Sunday, has spread to cities including Isfahan, Kermanshah and Kazerun. Tires, engine oil and diesel are effectively priced in dollars, the union said, and the rial fell past 2.8 million to the dollar this week, a record low. Drivers also face higher insurance, tolls and repair bills. "Until we get what we're owed, we won't haul freight," the union said.

Most of Iran's goods move by road, so a long strike can quickly reach factories, farms and markets, and the union warned that shortages of diesel and parts already threaten freight across the country. Farmers have voiced support for the drivers. In 2018, a truckers' strike over pay and costs spread to hundreds of cities, and the judiciary threatened strikers with harsh punishment.

outsiders.name: The Iran Watcher
outsiders.hook:
The U.S. is considering assassinating top Islamic Republic leaders and “hardliners” to speed up an agreement to end the war.

According to NBC News, supporters believe removing those figures could clear obstacles to a deal and demonstrate to surviving leaders that the U.S. can reach them at any time. Trump has reportedly made no decision.

NBC names no targets. Speculation could focus on Mojtaba Khamenei, IRGC commander Ahmad Vahidi and senior armed-forces figure Keyoumars Heydari. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf could also enter that discussion because of his IRGC background and political influence. None has been publicly confirmed as a target under this proposal.

The U.S. and Israel have already demonstrated their ability to penetrate the regime’s leadership security. Months of CIA and Israeli intelligence gathering helped locate Ali Khamenei and other senior figures. Reuters reported that Israeli intelligence detected a gathering of top officials, allowing the strikes to be timed around it. Khamenei and senior military leaders were killed.

But killing the leadership and changing the regime’s decisions are two different outcomes.

The Islamic Republic’s hostility toward the U.S. and Israel is embedded in its governing ideology, the IRGC and the security apparatus. Officials compete over power and tactics while remaining committed to preserving the same revolutionary system.

Across the 12-day and 40-day wars, Israel and the U.S. inflicted extraordinary losses on the Islamic Republic’s leadership. Israel said it killed more than 30 senior security officials during the 12-day war alone.

The subsequent U.S.-Israeli campaign killed Ali Khamenei and another layer of top military and political figures, demonstrating devastating intelligence penetration of the regime’s highest ranks.

Yet the system elevated Mojtaba Khamenei, replaced its commanders and continued fighting. The ability to eliminate its leaders has repeatedly outpaced the ability to change its decisions.

Removing commanders can disrupt operations, weaken coordination and alter internal calculations. It does not automatically change the institutions that select their replacements or the objectives those institutions pursue.

NBC reports that opponents within the administration fear further assassinations could harden surviving officials’ positions, undermine negotiations and increase threats against American officials.

The U.S. may be able to eliminate more leaders. Whether that produces an agreement depends on who succeeds them, who controls the security apparatus and whether those people have an incentive to compromise.

Masoud Pezeshkian, former foreign minister Mohammad Javad Zarif and former president Hassan Rouhani have repeatedly advocated engagement and an agreement with the U.S. One possible calculation is that removing their rivals could give figures like these greater influence, perhaps even a path to leading the Islamic Republic. That remains an interpretation of the proposal, rather than a succession plan reported by NBC.

Their willingness to negotiate matters. It does not fundamentally change their commitment to preserving the Islamic Republic. An agreement could reflect a different calculation about how to protect the same system, while its ideology, security institutions and mechanisms of repression endure.

Calling certain officials “hardliners” leaves the central question unanswered. What evidence shows that their replacements would make a different choice, and how much would that choice actually change the regime?

74 zweepslagen voor Parastoo Ahmadi omdat ze durft zingen zonder hijab. 🧕 Haar 29-jarige lichaam voor eeuwig verminkt door de ayatollahs en mullahs van het Iraanse regime. 

Vandaag worden er weer twee jongeren, Milad Armoun en Navid Najaran, opgehangen in Teheran. Omdat ze durven protesteren tegen het regime of zich niet houden aan de streng-islamitische kledingvoorschriften. Zo vergaat het jaarlijks duizenden jongeren. Het Iraanse regime is verantwoordelijk voor 80% (!) van alle executies wereldwijd.  

En onze media? Die hebben enkel inkt voor Gaza en ‘opperschurkenstaat’ Israël, de enige democratie in het Midden-Oosten. Het Iraanse regime behoort in het kamp van de slachtoffers van die grote boze oorlogsmisdadigers Donald Trump en Benjamin Netanyahu. Ocharme die ayatollahs toch. 

Marnix Peeters schreef zaterdag een treffende hoofddoekencolumn in HLN.

74 lashes for Parastoo Ahmadi because she dares to sing without a hijab. Her 29-year-old body scarred forever by the ayatollahs and mullahs of the Iranian regime.

Today two more young men, Milad Armoun and Navid Najaran, are being hanged in Tehran. Because they dared to protest against the regime or not follow the strict Islamic dress rules. That is what happens to thousands of young people every year. The Iranian regime is responsible for 80% (!) of all executions worldwide.

And our media? They only have ink for Gaza and "arch-rogue state" Israel, the only democracy in the Middle East. The Iranian regime belongs in the camp of victims of those big bad war criminals Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu. Poor ayatollahs.

Marnix Peeters wrote a sharp headscarf column in HLN on Saturday.

outsiders.hook:
Today is the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. 

Across the globe, women are bravely raising their voices against violence, while civil institutions, human rights organizations, and journalists speak out about the violated rights of women who need global solidarity to end this suffering. 

On this important day, let's speak of Iran and its women facing repression, domestic violence, systemic oppression, gender apartheid, patriarchal laws, flogging, imprisonment, torture, bullets, and the gallows. 

In Iran, we mark this day while lashes fall upon Parastoo Ahmadi for the sin of singing; amidst the pain of Navid Najaran and Milad Armoun held on death row for protesting during the 'Woman, Life, Freedom' movement—a movement born from the killing of Mahsa Jina Amini over mandatory hijab; with the murder of Sogand Sayyadi by her father; and with the repeated recitation of the names of women political prisoners facing execution. 

On this crucial day, I ask you to see, hear, and amplify the suffering of Iranian women. As a human rights defender, throughout the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence, I will write about women on death row, women murdered simply for their gender, and women arrested and tortured, who have never stopped fighting for their human rights.

Narges Mohammadi
25 Nov 2026

#EndViolenceAgainstWomen #WomensRights #ParastooAhmadi #MiladArmoon #NoToExecution #NavidNajaran

outsiders.name: Iran International English
outsiders.hook:
Iranian truck drivers entered a fifth day of strikes on Thursday, with their union saying drivers in 18 cities were refusing to haul freight at rates that have stayed flat as the cost of keeping a truck on the road has climbed.

The strike, which began on Sunday, has spread to cities including Isfahan, Kermanshah and Kazerun. Tires, engine oil and diesel are effectively priced in dollars, the union said, and the rial fell past 2.8 million to the dollar this week, a record low. Drivers also face higher insurance, tolls and repair bills. "Until we get what we're owed, we won't haul freight," the union said.

Most of Iran's goods move by road, so a long strike can quickly reach factories, farms and markets, and the union warned that shortages of diesel and parts already threaten freight across the country. Farmers have voiced support for the drivers. In 2018, a truckers' strike over pay and costs spread to hundreds of cities, and the judiciary threatened strikers with harsh punishment.
